title: Broccoli, cauliflower and carrots, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli, cauliflower and carrots are three vegetables often combined in cooking. When cooked by steaming or boiling with a small amount of added fat (oil or butter) they retain most of their vitamins and minerals, and the fat enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli and cauliflower belong to the cruciferous family and are rich in glucosinolates that support liver detoxification.
Carrots are one of the richest sources of beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.
This vegetable trio is common in traditional dishes worldwide, from French ratatouille to Asian stir‑fries.
Adding fat can increase the bioavailability of carotenoids in carrots up to 10‑12 times.
Short cooking times (5‑7 minutes) preserve more than 90 % of vitamin C in broccoli.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals such as sulforaphane in broccoli and quercetin in cauliflower help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports vision
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots converts to vitamin A, essential for eye health.

items.title: May reduce cardiovascular risk
items.content: Fiber and potassium aid normal blood pressure, while monounsaturated fats from oil support healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C in broccoli and cauliflower enhances immune cell function.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber from all three vegetables promotes gut motility and feeds beneficial gut microbes.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to broccoli or cauliflower.

items.title: Excess added fat
items.content: Using too much oil increases the dish’s calorie density and may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Vitamin C loss with prolonged boiling
items.content: Cooking vegetables for more than 10 minutes can degrade a portion of vitamin C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the vegetables as a side dish, add them to salads, stews or pasta. Steam for 5‑7 minutes, then lightly sauté with 1‑2 teaspoons of oil. Finish with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Store the cooked mixture in an airtight container for up to 3 days.
